column1: A week of badge swipes from a building nobody has audited since March. Three of the oddities in it are attacks. Two are not, and telling them apart is the lab.
Everything runs in this page. The log, the door reference and the badge list are simulated, so read them in any order and as many times as you need.

Finding something strange in a log is the easy half. A person working late and a badge used at 02:47 are both unusual, and only one of them is a problem. Decide what makes the difference before you decide which rows to flag.

All of them: the terminal labs hub. The exam asks you to write commands in its free-response question, and AP Cybersecurity practice puts the labs, the multiple choice and the free response in one place.
A real terminal, a pretend machine behind it, and a job to do. No install, no virtual machine, and no account needed to try one.

Each lab drops you into a filesystem with a brief and checks your work as you go. You navigate, read logs, inspect permissions and run commands, which is the same work the exam's free-response question asks you to reason about in writing.
Part C of the AP Cybersecurity free-response asks students to write a chmod command. Write is a CED task verb. These labs are practice for a graded part of the exam, not an extra.
